theme: The Passover instituted, the lamb and the blood
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 12:1-13:16. This is the central chapter of the Old Testament’s story of redemption. Read it slowly and with great care. Mark each instruction about the lamb, and notice what saves the people.
settingTheScene: Everything in the book of Exodus has been leading to this night. God is about to strike Egypt with the last plague, and he gives Israel a way to be protected: the Passover. It is the foundational event of Israel’s national life, and the Jewish people have kept the feast ever since. For Christians, it is the great shadow of the cross. Jesus died at Passover time, and he is called “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Understanding the Passover is the key to understanding what Jesus did.
observation: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you” (12:2).
Each household is to take a lamb “without blemish, a male a year old” (12:5).
The lamb is kept until the fourteenth day, and then “the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight” (12:6).
They are to take some of the blood “and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses” (12:7).
They are to eat the meat roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, “with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand” (12:8-11).
God says, “The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you” (12:13).
The feast of unleavened bread is to be kept as a memorial, and children are to be taught what it means (12:14-20, 26-27).
At midnight, the LORD struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, and “there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead” (12:29-30).
Pharaoh calls for Moses and says, “Up, go out from among my people” (12:31). A “mixed multitude” goes up with Israel (12:38).
God commands that every firstborn male be consecrated to him, and that every firstborn son be redeemed (13:1-2, 13).
interpretation:
The Passover is a story about substitution. In every house in Egypt, the firstborn was under a sentence of death. The difference between Israel and Egypt was not that Israel was more righteous. The difference was that, in Israel’s homes, a lamb had died in place of the firstborn son. The blood on the doorpost was the sign that the death had already occurred. When God saw it, he passed over.

Look at the details. The lamb is “without blemish.” It is chosen on the tenth day and kept in the house for four days, long enough for the family to become attached to it. It is killed by the whole community. Its blood is applied to the door. The meat is eaten. Every part of the ritual teaches something. The lamb is innocent. The death is public. The blood is a visible sign. And the family has to take it in.

Notice how little the people do. They do not fight, or earn their freedom. They do not even go out of the house. They shelter under the blood. This is why the New Testament uses the Passover to teach grace. We are saved not by what we do but by the blood of the Lamb applied to us.

The tone of the ritual is also important. They are to eat in haste, ready to leave. It is a night of judgment and of rescue. Salvation is not a calm event. But it is secure.

The Passover is also designed to be remembered. Three times in these chapters God tells the people to teach their children: “What do you mean by this service?” (12:26). The parents are to say, “It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt” (12:27). Redemption has to be told, again and again, to every generation.

Chapter 13 adds a second teaching: the firstborn belongs to God. Every firstborn son had to be redeemed, bought back, with the sacrifice of a lamb (13:13). A father would answer his son’s question by saying, “By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt” (13:14). Redemption creates ownership. Those who have been bought belong to the one who bought them.
connection: John the Baptist said of Jesus, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Jesus was crucified at Passover time, and John notes that “not one of his bones will be broken” (John 19:36, quoting Exodus 12:46). At the Last Supper, he took the Passover meal and gave it new meaning (Luke 22:14-20). Peter says we were ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18-19). Hebrews 11:28 says Moses kept the Passover “by faith.”
application:
When you take the Lord’s Supper, think of the Passover. You are not earning anything. You are receiving the benefits of a Lamb who died in your place.

Ask yourself if you are relying on the blood of Christ or on your own record. Say aloud, “When he sees the blood, he will pass over me.”

Think about how you can tell the story of your redemption to a child or a friend this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the blood of the Lamb, and say in your own words what it means that he passes over you.
Ask him to help you tell the story to someone younger.
Tell him you trust Christ and not yourself.
